A home espresso machine remains the most intense and expensive device I regularly operate before my first cup of coffee. This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from Americano to flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini.&quot;],[&quot;p&quot;,&quot;And yet the Jet&#x27;s easily accessible for anyone who can figure out &quot;,[&quot;a&quot;,{&quot;href&quot;:&quot;https://www.wired.com/gallery/iphone-buying-guide/&quot;,&quot;target&quot;:&quot;_blank&quot;,&quot;isExternal&quot;:false},&quot;an iPhone&quot;],&quot;, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You&#x27;ll be nose deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. For that, the price is not in every budget. Note, too, that manual milk steaming with the Jet&#x27;s powerful wand is still better than the automatic version. But lord, this machine makes delicious cups. And the cups come without me trying very hard. It hasn&#x27;t left my counter since it jaKDYU"><div><p>Sometimes the upgrade pick is the pick. The <a href="https://www.wired.com/review/breville-oracle-jet/" target="_blank">Breville Oracle Jet</a> is the espresso machine of the moment—the one that best threads that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness. It&#x27;s a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent <a data-offer-url="https://www.amazon.com/Baratza-Encore-Electric-Coffee-Grinder/dp/B0BW272XCV/" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank" data-aps-asin="B0BW272XCV" data-aps-asc-tag="w050b-20">Baratza Encore ESP ($200)</a>. This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from Americano to flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini.</p><p>And yet the Jet&#x27;s easily accessible for anyone who can figure out <a href="https://www.wired.com/gallery/iphone-buying-guide/" target="_blank">an iPhone</a>, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You&#x27;ll be nose deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. For that, the price is not in every budget. Note, too, that manual milk steaming with the Jet&#x27;s powerful wand is still better than the automatic version. But lord, this machine makes delicious cups. And the cups come without me trying very hard. It hasn&#x27;t left my counter since it This means well-extracted, café-grade espresso.</p><p>Note that the Silvia is notoriously sensitive, so it&#x27;s not for beginners. It&#x27;s also famously long-lasting, repairable, and able to be endlessly modified, and so it&#x27;s birthed its own society of cult devotees. Just like buying a Land Cruiser or a Jeep, you&#x27;ll end up with new friends. It remains among the most popular espresso machines in the world for good reason. The Barista Express produces consistent pressure for espresso, its steam wand is excellent, and the built-in grinder makes it an all-in-one device. Its mostly metal construction, easy cleaning, and other thoughtful touches make it a faithful companion: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu has been using one with no issues for half a decade.</p><p>But competitors have taken direct aim at the Express with impressive semiautomatic entries like the <a data-offer-url="https://www.amazon.com/Ninja-Integrated-Hands-Free-Cappuccinos-ES601/dp/B0D45PK5V4" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank" data-aps-asin="B0D45PK5V4" data-aps-asc-tag="w050b-20">Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ($599)</a> and the <a data-offer-url="https://www.williams-sonoma.com/products/delonghi-la-specialista-opera-espresso-machine-with-cold-brew/" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank">De&#x27;Longhi La Specialista Opera ($900)</a>. Each of these offers more options, including cold espresso, with similar grind quality. For now, the Barista Express&#x27;s long reliability keeps it on top as we keep testing durability on the Ninja and De&#x27;Longhi. UnifiedProductCardDescriptionWrapper-dyAmCu deqABF fxYvgV jaKDYU"><div><p>It&#x27;s tough to find a reliable espresso machine in the $200 range—and Italian coffee machine company De&#x27;Longhi has long dominated the WIRED Gear team&#x27;s favorite no-nonsense, low-budget espresso picks. The new De&#x27;Longhi Classic (previously branded as “Linea Classic”) is shiny chrome, with buttons for steam and your choice of single or double shots. It likewise sports a rare-at-this-price-point pressure gauge, a 15-bar pump, and an updated thermoblock system for fast heating.</p><p>The small touches matter. The surprisingly powerful steam wand has enough oomph to create some rudimentary latte art, if that’s your thing. And there&#x27;s enough clearance between the portafilter and drip tray to fit a coffee or cappuccino mug, as opposed to a tiny espresso cup. UnifiedProductCardDescriptionWrapper-dyAmCu deqABF fxYvgV jaKDYU"><div><p>This guide is mostly dedicated to machines that make more classic espresso—the finicky kind that&#x27;s harder to navigate and might leave coffee grounds on your counter. This sophisticated bean-to-cup <a href="https://www.wired.com/review/delonghi-rivelia-espresso-machine/" target="_blank">De&#x27;Longhi Rivelia</a> is a little different. It&#x27;s my top pick among super-automatic machines that&#x27;ll have you just fill a hopper with a half-bag of beans, then press a button. After helping you choose the right grinder settings, and asking how you like your coffee among well more than a dozen options, this touchscreen device will grind, and brew, and then froth up your milk for you.</p><p>Even the milk frother is about the easiest I&#x27;ve used, and it works with a single button-press once you&#x27;ve adjusted the foam density for drinks from dense flat white to frothy cappuccino. Heck, my mom was able to figure it out within a day, and so was my father. Even better, the Rivelia offers two swappable bean hoppers, an unheard-of luxury among similar devices that&#x27;ll allow you to switch easily to decaf late in the day.</p><p>Note, however, that automatic machines like this Rivelia tend to make somewhat different coffee from what you&#x27;ll get from other machines on this list. It grinds a bit coarser, leading to less unpredictability but also less intensity. If you&#x27;re a milk lover, this likely won&#x27;t matter much—and you may instead prize the simple ease with which you can have a frothing latte. Vodka lovers will find the same, when mixing cold espresso shots with the data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank"><strong>Meraki Espresso Machine for $2,000:</strong></a> Meraki is a young Hong Kong–based company. Last year it was still Kickstarting funds for its debut <a href="https://www.wired.com/review/meraki-espresso-maker/" target="_blank">Meraki Espresso Machine</a>. But the company started off with a bang, with a premium semiautomatic double-boiler machine offering features you don&#x27;t find even in machines that cost hundreds more. This means a Timemore grinder that&#x27;ll grind by weight within two-tenths of a gram precision. PID temperature control. Easy pre-infusion. A quiet rotary pump. Another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. A powerful steam wand that regulates the temperature of froth within about 3 degrees for whatever milk drinks strike your fancy. A tamper with satisfying heft, and a tamping station that feels like luxury. Frankly, despite having to overrotate the portafilter for proper fit, it&#x27;s a contender among our top picks—though I&#x27;m still testing durability on the device.</p><ad position="mid-content"></ad><p><a data-offer-url="https://www.amazon.com/Ninja-Integrated-Hands-Free-Cappuccinos-ES601/dp/B0D45PK5V4/" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank" data-aps-asin="B0D45PK5V4" data-aps-asc-tag="w050b-20"><strong>Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier for $599:</strong></a> Ninja has already released an upgraded <a data-offer-url="https://www.crateandbarrel.com/ninja-luxe-cafe-pro-series-espresso-machine/s505427" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank">Ninja Cafe Luxe Pro version ($750)</a> after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the <a data-offer-url="https://www.wired.com/review/luxe-cafe-premier-series-automatic-espresso-machine/" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank">Cafe Luxe Premier</a>, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED&#x27;s mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.</p><native-ad position="sponsor-product" shouldDisplayLabel="true"></native-ad><p><a data-offer-url="https://www.amazon.com/DeLonghi-Specialista-Commercial-style-Cappuccino-EC9555M/dp/B0D1TY3H2J/" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://cna.st/affiliate-&quot;}" href="https://cna.st/affiliate-" rel="sponsored" target="_blank" data-aps-asin="B0D1TY3H2J" data-aps-asc-tag="w050b-20"><strong>De&#x27;Longhi La Specialista Opera for $900</strong>:</a> Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It&#x27;s the best De&#x27;Longhi espresso machine I&#x27;ve tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.</p><native-ad position="in-content" data-aps-asin="B08C96BG9H" data-aps-asc-tag="w050b-20"><strong>De&#x27;Longhi Stilosa for $150</strong>:</a> The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It&#x27;s still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You&#x27;re not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it&#x27;s a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you&#x27;ll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never showed signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. It&#x27;s a good machine, but I&#x27;d upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.</p><inline-embed name="faq" attrs="[object Object]" childTypes="callout:anchor,callout:accordion" contentType="callout:faq"><div style="outline:none" id="FAQ" tabindex="-1"><h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2></div><div name="accordion" class="AccordionWrapper-hsYVHT bgMFty"><div class="AccordionItemWrapper-eWlGuu eNwKZf"><div class="AccordionContainer-foSklP iRHdCZ"><div data-testid="accordion-item-container" class="AccordionItemContainer-ywYcO eQgPvY"><div class="AccordionItemContainerLabel-ioTxOM diANax"><p>How Do We Test and Evaluate Espresso Machines?</p></div><button class="BaseButton-lbLhfD ButtonWrapper-igqDZ gTIqfM hKIiJv button button--utility AccordionItemContainerButton-eSsfaw Wvvyo" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;Button&quot;}" data-testid="Button" role="button" type="button"><span class="ButtonLabel-cyWivE hvohFn button__label">AccordionItemContainerButton</span><div class="ButtonIconWrapper-gzKJtq bQqPLN button__icon-container"><svg class="ButtonIcon-bdIQNJ jKYSoZ button-icon icon icon-large-chevron" focusable="false" width="32" height="32" viewBox="0 0 32 32" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><title>LargeChevron</title><path fill-rule="evenodd" clip-rule="evenodd" d="m1.47 10.53 1.06-1.06L16 22.94 29.47 9.47l1.06 1.06L16 25.06 1.47 10.53Z" fill="#000"></path></svg></div></button></div><div class="AccordionItemContainerContent-bPelIb leTzLN opening-animation"><div><p>Over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my <a data-offer-url="https://www.wweek.com/culture/2017/11/07/portland-has-deeper-cups-than-any-coffee-city-in-america/" class="external-link" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;ExternalLink&quot;,&quot;outgoingURL&quot;:&quot;https://www.wweek.com/culture/2017/11/07/portland-has-deeper-cups-than-any-coffee-city-in-america/&quot;}" href="https://www.wweek.com/culture/2017/11/07/portland-has-deeper-cups-than-any-coffee-city-in-america/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon.</a> Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include <a href="https://www.wired.com/author/jaina-grey/" target="_blank">Jaina Grey</a>, <a href="https://www.wired.com/author/jeffrey-van-camp/" target="_blank">Jeffrey Van Camp</a>, <a href="https://www.wired.com/author/kat-merck/" target="_blank">Kat Merck</a>, <a href="https://www.wired.com/author/tyler-shane/" target="_blank">Tyler Shane</a>, <a href="https://www.wired.com/author/pete-cottell/" target="_blank">Pete Cottell</a>, and <a href="https://www.wired.com/author/scott-gilbertson/" target="_blank">Scott Gilbertson</a>.</p><p>On each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four drinks, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.</p><p>I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it. (Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner.)</p><p>What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.</p><p>I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s <em>possible</em> is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.</p><p>On machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.</p><p>On any semiautomatic machine that decide the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you&#x27;re getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.</p><p>I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.</p></div></div></div></div><div class="AccordionItemWrapper-eWlGuu eNwKZf"><div class="AccordionContainer-foSklP iRHdCZ"><div data-testid="accordion-item-container" class="AccordionItemContainer-ywYcO eQgPvY"><div class="AccordionItemContainerLabel-ioTxOM diANax"><p>How We Select Espresso Machines to Test</p></div><button class="BaseButton-lbLhfD ButtonWrapper-igqDZ gTIqfM hKIiJv button button--utility AccordionItemContainerButton-eSsfaw Wvvyo" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;Button&quot;}" data-testid="Button" role="button" type="button"><span class="ButtonLabel-cyWivE hvohFn button__label">AccordionItemContainerButton</span><div class="ButtonIconWrapper-gzKJtq bQqPLN button__icon-container"><svg class="ButtonIcon-bdIQNJ jKYSoZ button-icon icon icon-large-chevron" focusable="false" width="32" height="32" viewBox="0 0 32 32" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><title>LargeChevron</title><path fill-rule="evenodd" clip-rule="evenodd" d="m1.47 10.53 1.06-1.06L16 22.94 29.47 9.47l1.06 1.06L16 25.06 1.47 10.53Z" fill="#000"></path></svg></div></button></div><div class="AccordionItemContainerContent-bPelIb leTzLN opening-animation"><div><p>In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De&#x27;Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.</p><p>I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most users. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.</p><p>But I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.</p><p>This means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.</p><p>The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.</p><p>But hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.</p></div></div></div></div><div class="AccordionItemWrapper-eWlGuu eNwKZf"><div class="AccordionContainer-foSklP iRHdCZ"><div data-testid="accordion-item-container" class="AccordionItemContainer-ywYcO eQgPvY"><div class="AccordionItemContainerLabel-ioTxOM diANax"><p>What Beans Are Best for Espresso?</p></div><button class="BaseButton-lbLhfD ButtonWrapper-igqDZ gTIqfM hKIiJv button button--utility AccordionItemContainerButton-eSsfaw Wvvyo" data-event-click="{&quot;element&quot;:&quot;Button&quot;}" data-testid="Button" role="button" type="button"><span class="ButtonLabel-cyWivE hvohFn button__label">AccordionItemContainerButton</span><div class="ButtonIconWrapper-gzKJtq bQqPLN button__icon-container"><svg class="ButtonIcon-bdIQNJ jKYSoZ button-icon icon icon-large-chevron" focusable="false" width="32" height="32" viewBox="0 0 32 32" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><title>LargeChevron</title><path fill-rule="evenodd" clip-rule="evenodd" d="m1.47 10.53 1.06-1.06L16 22.94 29.47 9.47l1.06 1.06L16 25.06 1.47 10.53Z" fill="#000"></path></svg></div></button></div><div class="AccordionItemContainerContent-bPelIb leTzLN opening-animation"><div><p>First off, there&#x27;s no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.</p><p>But traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that&#x27;s often what they mean.</p><p>Does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.</p><p>It&#x27;s up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you&#x27;ll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.</p><p>One thing that&#x27;s true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They&#x27;ll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they&#x27;ve begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.</p><p>Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you&#x27;ll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can&#x27;t find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they&#x27;re not fresh. And your espresso will be worse.</p></div></div></div></div><div class="AccordionItemWrapper-eWlGuu eNwKZf"><div class="AccordionContainer-foSklP iRHdCZ"><div data-testid="accordion-item-container" But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts."],["p","I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it. (Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner.)"],["p","What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk."],["p","On machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent."],["p","On any semiautomatic machine that decide the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again."],["p","I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood."]]],["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-item","attrs":{"opened":"true"},"childTypes":["callout:accordion-header","callout:accordion-panel"]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-item"},["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-header","attrs":{},"childTypes":[]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-header"},["p","How We Select Espresso Machines to Test"]],["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-panel","attrs":{},"childTypes":[]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-panel"},["p","In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations."],["p","I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most users. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest."],["p","But I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you."],["p","This means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal."],["p","The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino."],["p","But hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better."]]],["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-item","attrs":{"opened":"true"},"childTypes":["callout:accordion-header","callout:accordion-panel"]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-item"},["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-header","attrs":{},"childTypes":[]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-header"},["p","What Beans Are Best for Espresso?"]],["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-panel","attrs":{},"childTypes":[]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-panel"},["p","First off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso."],["p","But traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean."],["p","Does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries."],["p","It's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans."],["p","One thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors."],["p","Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse."]]],["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-item","attrs":{"opened":"true"},"childTypes":["callout:accordion-header","callout:accordion-panel"]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-item"},["inline-embed",{"props":{"name":"accordion-header","attrs":{},"childTypes":[]},"ref":"","type":"callout:accordion-header"},["p","Espresso
